Here’s why this creates so much distress:

-The ACC over-detects errors, conflicts, and uncertainty, even when there is no real problem or the risk is extremely low.

It generates an exaggerated “something is wrong” or “I must fix this now” signal.

A normal, passing doubt (“Did I lock the door properly?” or “What if these thoughts mean I’m a bad person?”) gets amplified into an urgent, distressing alarm.

Neutral situations or minor imperfections feel like critical mistakes that demand immediate action.

This hyper-responsiveness creates a constant sense of unease, incompleteness, or impending doom as a lot of patients descirbe.

It drives the intense urge to perform compulsions (checking, washing, repeating, mental reviewing) to temporarily silence the alarm and reduce anxiety.

The hyperactivity is especially strong during error-related tasks or symptom provocation.

Studies show greater activation in the rostral ACC during errors, and this activity often correlates with symptom severity (higher Y-BOCS scores).

It can occur even when symptoms aren’t actively flaring, suggesting it’s a trait-like feature of OCD.

Because the ACC is tightly linked to the salience network (with the insula), it can make internal thoughts or bodily sensations feel overly important or threatening.

This interacts with the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) and striatum in the CSTC loop, turning a small signal into a self-reinforcing cycle: obsession → amplified “error/uncertainty” signal → compulsion → short relief → repeat.

So if the OFC is the security guard, the ACC is an overly sensitive smoke detector.

VIDEO — STATIC SHOT: KARIMA FROM BEHIND IN THE CORRIDOR, BUTTERFLY HOPPING BETWEEN HER FINGERS

SCENE CONTEXT: The same composition as the still frame, now alive. Karima stands in the middle of the dim hotel corridor with her back to the camera, cropped at the knees, her hip cocked, her head turned into a clean side profile. One hand hugs her own hip; the other is raised near her face, fingers lightly spread, and the black butterfly steps and hops delicately from one of her fingertips to the next, wings opening and closing as it resettles. The camera never moves, and the whole frame is canted so the corridor slopes down to the left.

FORMAT
One continuous shot, 5 seconds, 9:16 vertical, full photorealism, cinematic color grade — warm amber and deep shadow, shallow depth of field, real film-like contrast. No on-screen text, no captions, no subtitles, no music.

THE SEVEN MOST IMPORTANT RULES ON THIS SHOT

RULE ONE — THE CAMERA IS COMPLETELY STATIC AND LOCKED OFF FOR THE ENTIRE SHOT. HARD, MANDATORY. No pan, no tilt, no dolly, no zoom, no handheld drift or shake at any point — one fixed frame from first to last. The only movement in the image comes from Karima and the butterfly.
IF THE CAMERA MOVES IN ANY WAY, THE GENERATION IS WRONG. HARD FAILURE CONDITION.

RULE TWO — SHE STANDS WITH HER BACK TO THE CAMERA, CROPPED AT THE KNEES, CENTERED IN THE CORRIDOR, AND STAYS THERE. She never turns toward the camera, never walks, never changes her position in frame — she holds her stance for the whole shot, with the corridor receding symmetrically past her on both sides and the frame cut at her knees.
IF SHE TURNS TOWARD THE CAMERA, WALKS, MOVES OUT OF THE CENTER OF THE CORRIDOR, OR IS FRAMED FULL-LENGTH INSTEAD OF AT THE KNEES, THE GENERATION IS WRONG.

RULE THREE — HER HIP STAYS COCKED AND HER HEAD STAYS IN CLEAN SIDE PROFILE THROUGHOUT. Her weight rests on one leg with the opposite hip pushed out in a relaxed contrapposto; her head remains turned fully to the side so her face reads in true profile for the entire shot — the line of her nose, lips and chin, her lashes and the edge of her grey smoky eye. She may blink and breathe, and her gaze may drift a few degrees toward the butterfly, but her head never rotates back toward the camera or into a three-quarter angle.
IF HER FACE TURNS OUT OF PROFILE AT ANY POINT, OR HER STANCE STRAIGHTENS INTO A SQUARE, STIFF POSTURE, THE GENERATION IS WRONG.

RULE FOUR — ONE HAND HUGS HER HIP, THE OTHER STAYS RAISED NEAR HER FACE WITH THE BUTTERFLY ON IT. Her lower arm stays crossed in front of her, hand wrapped around her own hip and thigh in a self-embrace, unmoving apart from the smallest natural settle. Her other arm stays lifted, elbow bent, hand held near the level of her face, fingers extended and lightly spread, held patiently still so the butterfly can move across them — she does not lower the hand, wave it, or grab at the butterfly.
IF THE RAISED HAND DROPS BELOW SHOULDER HEIGHT, IF THE HUGGING HAND LEAVES HER HIP, OR IF SHE REACHES FOR OR GRASPS THE BUTTERFLY, THE GENERATION IS WRONG.

RULE FIVE — THE BUTTERFLY HOPS DELICATELY FROM ONE FINGERTIP TO ANOTHER, AT LEAST TWICE, AND NEVER FLIES AWAY. It moves in small, careful, deliberate steps and short hops: a brief flutter of the wings, a light lift of only a few centimetres, and a soft landing on the next finger, its legs visibly gripping, its wings opening and closing slowly to balance after each landing. It stays on her hand for the entire shot — it never leaves frame, never lands on her face or hair, never flies off.
IF THE BUTTERFLY FLIES AWAY, LEAVES HER HAND, LANDS ANYWHERE ELSE, OR STAYS FROZEN ON ONE FINGER FOR THE WHOLE SHOT WITHOUT HOPPING AT LEAST TWICE, THE GENERATION IS WRONG.

RULE SIX — THE HORIZON IS DELIBERATELY TILTED DOWN TO THE LEFT AND STAYS THAT WAY. The whole frame is canted so the corridor's ceiling line, wainscot line, floor edges and carpet runner slope downward toward the left side of the frame, the left edge sitting lower than the right by roughly 8–12 degrees, held perfectly constant for all 5 seconds — the tilt never corrects itself or drifts.
IF THE FRAME IS LEVEL, IF THE TILT SLOPES DOWN TO THE RIGHT, OR IF THE TILT CHANGES DURING THE SHOT, THE GENERATION IS WRONG.

RULE SEVEN — THE CORRIDOR IS OTHERWISE EMPTY AND NO CAMERA OR PHONE IS EVER VISIBLE. No second person, no figure in the background, no reflection of anyone, no visible recording device anywhere in frame.
IF ANY OTHER PERSON, FIGURE, OR CAMERA DEVICE APPEARS, THE GENERATION IS WRONG.

ACTIVE REFERENCES

[tag your character sheet here] — KARIMA, CHARACTER IDENTITY AND WARDROBE ONLY. Take from it her exact established face (read here in profile), her dark hair in two long braids with small silver rings threaded along them, her chin-length side-swept fringe, her cool grey smoky eye makeup, her multiple ear piercings with asymmetric hoop earrings, her finger rings, and her outfit: the black structured cropped jacket with its metal ring hardware over the sheer ivory lace blouse with its closed ruffled high collar and lace cuffs, with black wide trousers.
TAKE NOTHING ELSE FROM [tag your character sheet here]: not its plain grey studio background or its flat studio lighting, not its front-facing symmetrical standing pose, not its full-length framing.

<<<image_3>>> — LOCATION ONLY. Take from it the old-style hotel corridor: the dark wood paneling and wainscoting, the mirrored rows of tall dark doors and warm brass wall sconces down both walls, the long patterned carpet runner, the closed double door at the far end, and the one-point perspective receding to a vanishing point.
TAKE NOTHING ELSE FROM <<<image_3>>>: not its perfectly level horizon (this shot is tilted per Rule Six), not any camera movement, not any people.

<<<image_2>>> — BUTTERFLY DESIGN ONLY. Take from it the established black butterfly: deep matte-black wings with fine vein texture, the tailed hindwing shape, the long slender antennae, and the concentric honey-cream eye-marking centered on each upper wing.
TAKE NOTHING ELSE FROM <<<image_2>>>: not its white product background, not its flat pinned symmetry — here it is alive, stepping and hopping across her fingers with its wings opening and closing.

CHARACTERS
KARIMA — the only person in the shot, seen from behind, cropped at the knees, holding her stance per Rules Two, Three and Four.
THE BUTTERFLY — the established black butterfly, moving across her fingertips per Rule Five.

LOCATION
The old-style hotel corridor described above — dim, warm, symmetrical, its rows of doors and sconces receding behind her toward the closed far door, the patterned carpet runner leading down the centre beneath her feet.

CAMERA AND COMPOSITION
A fixed, locked-off viewpoint set in the corridor a few metres behind her at roughly chest height, looking straight down the hallway with her silhouette centred against the perspective, canted per Rule Six. Shallow depth of field holds her and the butterfly sharp while the corridor behind softens into warm bokeh, the sconces blooming into soft round highlights. Focus stays on her raised hand and profile for the whole shot.

ACTION TIMING — 5 SECONDS
0.0–1.0s: The held frame — Karima stands still in her cocked stance, head in profile, one hand around her hip, the other raised near her face; the butterfly sits on her index fingertip, wings slowly opening and closing once as it balances. Her braids and a loose strand settle faintly with her breathing.
1.0–1.8s: The butterfly takes its first small hop — a brief flutter, a lift of only a few centimetres, and a soft landing on the next finger, legs gripping, wings spreading wide for balance then easing part-way closed.
1.8–2.6s: It settles, antennae moving slightly, wings opening and closing once in a slow beat; Karima's gaze drifts a few degrees toward it without her head leaving profile, and she blinks once.
2.6–3.4s: The second hop — the butterfly steps forward, half-opens its wings and lifts onto the next fingertip, landing lightly and rocking a fraction before steadying, its wings flaring open to show both eye-markings.
3.4–4.3s: It stays there, wings slowly opening and closing; her raised fingers adjust by the smallest amount to keep it steady, and the silver rings on her braids catch a flicker of the sconce light as she breathes.
4.3–5.0s: A held final beat — the butterfly's wings settle half-open, Karima remains motionless in profile, the corridor glowing softly behind her, the frame still canted and locked.

PHYSICS
The butterfly's hops carry real insect weight: a quick wing-flutter for lift, a short low arc, visible leg contact on landing, and a small wobble as it rebalances before the wings settle. Her fingers give the faintest micro-adjustment under each landing. Her breathing moves her shoulders subtly; the braids and loose strands shift only slightly, never swinging.

LIGHTING
Warm amber sconce light from both walls, falling on her shoulders, the side of her face in profile, and the raised hand with the butterfly, leaving her back and jacket in rich shadow; the corridor behind glows in soft receding pools of light with deep darkness between them; constant exposure and white balance for the whole shot — no flicker, no change in light level.

AUDIO
Diegetic only — deep corridor room tone, the faint papery flutter of the butterfly's wings on each hop, the small rustle of fabric as she breathes. No music, no voices, no subtitles, no on-screen text.

COUNT
Exactly one character, one butterfly, at least two finger-to-finger hops, one corridor, one fixed canted camera frame, zero camera movement, zero other people, zero visible devices, zero text overlays.

BANS
Camera inversions: any pan, tilt, dolly, zoom, handheld drift or shake — hard rule.
Pose inversions: turning toward camera, walking, three-quarter or front-on face, square stiff hips, dropping the raised hand, releasing her hip, grabbing at the butterfly.
Framing inversions: full-length or waist-up framing instead of the knee crop, her figure drifting off-centre in the corridor.
Tilt inversions: a level frame, a tilt sloping down to the right, or a tilt that changes during the shot.
Butterfly inversions: flying away, leaving her hand, landing on her face or hair, staying frozen on one finger with no hops, or fluttering so fast the eye-markings never read.
Identity inversions: any change to her established face, braids, fringe, piercings, earrings, rings, or outfit from [tag your character sheet here].
Population inversions: any second person, background figure, or reflection of one.
Lighting inversions: bright daylight, cool white light, flat shadowless lighting, or any flicker/change in light level.
Style inversions: no illustration, no painterly rendering, no CGI-smooth or plastic skin, no anime proportions.
General: no on-screen text, no logos, no watermark, no music, no visible camera or phone.
